nameStory: The Northern Threetooth gets its distinctive name from the three small tooth-like projections inside its shell opening, which are unique identifying features among New England land snails. The 'northern' part distinguishes it from its southern cousin, the Magnolia Threetooth, helping scientists and naturalists know which region they're exploring.
description: The Northern Threetooth is a small, air-breathing land snail that makes its home in the forests and woodlands of New England. Like all land snails, it carries a coiled shell on its back and glides along on a muscular foot, leaving a silvery slime trail behind. These terrestrial snails are part of the large group called pulmonate gastropods, which means they breathe air through a simple lung rather than gills. Though tiny, they play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down decaying plant matter.

idTips.label: Three-tooth shell opening
idTips.description: Look inside the shell opening for three small, white tooth-like projections that feel hard and smooth to the touch - this is the snail's signature feature

idTips.label: Shell size and shape
idTips.description: Shell is small and dome-shaped, typically fitting comfortably on your thumbnail with room to spare

idTips.label: Shell color and texture
idTips.description: Shell appears brownish or tan with a slightly glossy surface that feels smooth when dry but may have fine growth lines you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Coiling pattern
idTips.description: Shell spirals tightly in a low dome shape rather than forming a tall spire, creating a flattened appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Slime trail
idTips.description: When active, leaves a thin, silvery mucus trail that feels slippery and sticky between your fingers

habitat: Northern Threeteeth prefer moist, deciduous and mixed forests with rich, well-drained soil full of leaf litter and decaying organic matter. Look for them under fallen logs, among moss-covered rocks, or nestled in the damp leaf litter of maple, oak, and beech forests. They favor areas with consistent moisture but good drainage, often on gentle slopes or in protected valleys.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and moisture increases from snowmelt. Look for fresh slime trails on logs and rocks in the early morning.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid nights and after rain showers. During dry spells, they retreat deep into leaf litter or under logs where it stays moist.
seasonality.fall: Very active in the damp conditions as leaves fall and decay. This is often the best time to spot them as they feed on decomposing organic matter.
seasonality.winter: Become dormant and seal themselves into their shells with a thin membrane. Look for them hibernating under deep leaf litter or in soil crevices.

funFact: Northern Threeteeth are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, but they still need to find a partner to mate - they essentially take turns being both mom and dad!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small woodland snails, but the three teeth inside the shell opening are diagnostic - no other New England land snail has exactly this feature. Memory trick: 'Three teeth, three-tooth' - count the projections inside the shell opening.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'teeth,' the projections inside the shell aren't used for eating at all - they're actually barriers that help protect the snail when it retreats into its shell. The real feeding happens with a rasping tongue called a radula that scrapes up tiny bits of decaying plant matter.
compareHints: The Northern Threetooth differs from its closest relative, the Magnolia Threetooth, primarily by geographic range - the Magnolia Threetooth is found in southeastern states rather than New England. Within New England's snail community, the three internal teeth immediately separate it from all other small woodland snails, which either lack teeth entirely or have different numbers and arrangements of these shell projections.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the northern threetooth, the magnolia threetooth typically has a slightly more flattened shell profile and shows a stronger preference for rich deciduous forests rather than mixed or disturbed habitats.
